title: Groundnut Stew
subtitle: West African chicken stew with peanut sauce
excerpt: Groundnut stew is a West African classic. Chicken is cooked in a rich tomato and peanut sauce that is at once savoury, sweet, and slightly nutty. It is one of the most widely eaten stews across Ghana, Nigeria, and Senegal. The peanut adds body and richness without being heavy.
sourceNotes: Groundnut stew -- also known as peanut soup or maafe -- has been cooked across West and Central Africa for centuries. Peanuts arrived in Africa from South America via the Portuguese in the 16th century and were adopted rapidly into local cooking. Today versions exist from Senegal to Ghana to Cameroon to Sudan.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes well for up to 2 months. Reheat gently and stir well as the sauce can separate.

content.text: Use a natural, smooth peanut butter with no added sugar or salt for the best result. Stir the peanut butter with a little hot stock before adding it to the pot -- this helps it dissolve without lumping.

items.prepNote: use red palm oil if available

content.text: Season the chicken. Heat the oil in a large pot over high heat. Brown the chicken on all sides for 5 minutes. Remove and set aside.
Cook the onion in the same oil for 7 minutes. Add the garlic and ginger. Cook 2 minutes.
Add the tinned tomatoes and chilli flakes. Cook for 8 minutes until the sauce thickens.
Stir the peanut butter into 200ml of the warm stock until smooth. Pour this into the pot along with the remaining stock.
Return the chicken. Add salt. Bring to a simmer, then cover and cook over low heat for 30 minutes until the chicken is tender and the sauce is thick.
Taste and adjust salt. Serve with rice or fufu.

items.symptom: Sauce is very grainy or lumpy
items.cause: Peanut butter was not dissolved before adding
items.fix: Always whisk the peanut butter into warm stock first before pouring into the pot

items.cause: The peanut butter thickens as it simmers
items.fix: Add hot water or stock a little at a time and stir until you reach the right consistency
Use unsweetened peanut butter; add a little chilli or lemon juice to cut the sweetness

content.text: Groundnut stew appears in different forms across West Africa. In Ghana it is called groundnut soup and is eaten with fufu at celebrations and family meals. In Senegal the peanut-based stew is called maafe. In Cameroon it is made with palm butter. All versions share the combination of peanut, tomato, and slow-cooked meat.
